title: Abigail Adams
description: First Lady of the United States from 1797 to 1801
wiki_lead:
Abigail Adams (née Smith; 22 November [O.S. 11 November] 1744 – October 28, 1818) was the wife and closest advisor of John Adams, the second president of the United States, and the mother of John Quincy Adams, the sixth president of the United States. She is widely considered to be an influential figure in the founding of the United States, and was both the first second lady and second first lady of the United States, although such titles were not used at the time. She and Barbara Bush are the only two women in American history who were both the wife of a U.S. president and the mother of another U.S. president.
Abigail Adams's life is one of the most documented of the first ladies. Many of the letters she wrote to John Adams while he was in Philadelphia as a delegate in the Continental Congress, prior to and during the Revolutionary War, document the closeness and versatility of their relationship. John Adams frequently sought the advice of Abigail on many matters, and their letters are filled with intellectual discussions on government and politics. Her letters also serve as eyewitness accounts of the home front of the Revolutionary War.
Surveys of historians conducted periodically by the Siena College Research Institute since 1982 have consistently found Adams to rank as one of the three most highly regarded first ladies by historians.

Early life and family (1744–1759)

Abigail Adams was born on November 22, 1744, at the North Parish Congregational Church in Weymouth, Massachusetts, to William Smith and Elizabeth (née Quincy) Smith. On her mother's side, she was descended from the Quincy political family, a well-known political family in the Massachusetts colony. Through her mother she was a cousin of Dorothy Quincy, who was married to John Hancock. Adams was also the great-granddaughter of John Norton, founding pastor of Old Ship Church in Hingham, Massachusetts, the only remaining 17th-century Puritan meetinghouse in Massachusetts. Smith married Elizabeth Quincy in 1740, and together they had three daughters and a son; Abigail was the second child. As with several of her ancestors, Adams's father was a liberal Congregational minister: a leader in a Yankee society that held its clergy in high esteem. Smith did not focus his preaching on predestination or original sin; instead he emphasized the importance of reason and morality. In October 1775 his wife Elizabeth, with whom he had been married for 35 years, died. In 1784, at age 77, Smith died.
The Smith family were slaveholders and are known to have owned at least four people. A slave named Phoebe took a caretaking role to Abigail and other children; later on she would work as a paid servant for Abigail after she became free. Abigail would come to express anti-slavery beliefs as an adult.

grok_lead: Abigail Adams (November 11, 1744 â October 28, 1818) was the wife of John Adams, the second president of the United States, and the mother of John Quincy Adams, the sixth president. She served as the second First Lady from 1797 to 1801, during which she hosted social functions in the newly constructed but unfinished White House and advocated for public education and the abolition of slavery. Born Abigail Smith in Weymouth, Massachusetts, to a prominent family, she married John Adams on October 25, 1764, and managed their family farm and finances during his frequent absences for legal, revolutionary, and diplomatic duties. Throughout the American Revolution, Adams corresponded extensively with her husband, offering political advice and insights into homefront conditions, including her famous 1776 plea to "remember the ladies" in the new laws, warning against granting men unlimited power over women. She also participated in interrogating suspected Loyalist women and supported independence efforts despite personal hardships like smallpox outbreaks and economic strain. As Second Lady from 1789 to 1797, she influenced Federalist policies and defended her husband's positions, including the Alien and Sedition Acts, while critiquing figures like Alexander Hamilton. Her letters, preserved in archives, reveal a sharp intellect and commitment to republican principles, making her one of the most documented women of the founding era.
